scenes.title: A whole world inside your head
Pictures at bedtime
scenes.poem:
At seven, when I go to bed,
I find such pictures in my head;
lines: At seven, when I go to bed,
I find such pictures in my head;

scenes.title: Beauty, magic, and adventure
lines: Castles with dragons prowling round,
Gardens where magic fruits are found;
Fair ladies prisoned in a tower,
Or lost in an enchanted bower;

scenes.title: The land of dreams
scenes.poem:
While gallant horsemen ride by streams
That border all this land of dreams
I find, so clearly in my head
At seven, when I go to bed.
lines: While gallant horsemen ride by streams

scenes.title: Morning changes the picture
scenes.poem:
At seven, when I wake again,
The magic land I seek in vain;
A chair stands where the castle frowned,
The carpet hides the garden ground,
lines: At seven, when I wake again,
The magic land I seek in vain;

The carpet hides the garden ground,

scenes.title: The ordinary room returns
scenes.poem:
No fairies trip across the floor,
Boots, and not horsemen, flank the door,
And where the blue streams rippling ran
Is now a bath and water-can;

scenes.title: Looking for the magic
scenes.poem:
I seek the magic land in vain
At seven, when I wake again.

beats.text: Have you ever imagined a whole adventure while lying in bed?
Perhaps your ordinary room seemed to disappear, and a completely different world took its place.
In ‘A Child’s Thought’, Robert Louis Stevenson lets us enter a child’s imagination.
At bedtime, the child pictures a magical world.
When morning comes, something changes.
Let’s read a little at a time.
As we listen, keep one question in mind: what can the child find in imagination that cannot be found in the room?
At seven, when I go to bed,
I find such pictures in my head;
The child is speaking directly to us, using the word ‘I’.
Seven is bedtime here.
These ‘pictures’ are scenes in the child’s mind.
They are not photographs hanging on the wall!
The phrase ‘in my head’ tells us where to look: inside the imagination.
The word ‘find’ makes these pictures sound like discoveries.
The child is about to tell us what this inner world contains.
Castles with dragons prowling round,
Gardens where magic fruits are found;
Fair ladies prisoned in a tower,
Or lost in an enchanted bower;
What a busy imagination!
We have castles, dragons, magical gardens, and ladies in mysterious places.
‘Prowling’ means moving quietly and carefully.
The dragons seem watchful.
The magic fruit adds wonder to the gardens.
Here, ‘fair’ means beautiful.
‘Prisoned’ means imprisoned, or kept captive.
The ladies may be shut in a tower, or lost in an ‘enchanted bower’.
A bower is a pleasant shaded place under trees, and ‘enchanted’ means under a magic spell.
Which details make this world seem different from an ordinary garden?
The dragons, magic fruit, and enchanted bower belong to a world of fantasy.
It combines beauty with adventure and a hint of danger.
The poem gives us ingredients for an exciting story, without telling us a whole rescue or battle.
While gallant horsemen ride by streams
That border all this land of dreams
I find, so clearly in my head
At seven, when I go to bed.
‘Gallant’ means brave.
The horsemen ride beside streams—small, narrow rivers.
These streams ‘border’ the dream land: they run along its edges.
The final two lines bring us back to the child in bed.
The words ‘so clearly’ show how vivid the pictures are.
Something can feel very clear in your imagination without being physically in front of you.
Notice that the stanza ends with the same bedtime line that began it.
We have travelled around the dream world and returned to the moment when the child imagines it.
At seven, when I wake again,
The magic land I seek in vain;
A chair stands where the castle frowned,
The carpet hides the garden ground,
Now the child wakes.
‘Seek’ means look for, and ‘in vain’ means without success.
The child looks for the magical land but cannot find it.
What occupies the places where the castle and garden seemed to be?
A chair is there instead of the castle, and a carpet covers the place of the garden.
These are familiar objects in the waking room.
The poem is comparing two ways the child experiences the same surroundings.
The garden is not really hidden underneath the carpet!
The imagined landscape has given way to the ordinary room.
Keep an eye on ‘the castle frowned’.
We will come back to that interesting description.
No fairies trip across the floor,
Boots, and not horsemen, flank the door,
And where the blue streams rippling ran
Is now a bath and water-can;
There are no fairies moving across the floor.
Here, ‘trip’ means move lightly, with quick little steps.
It does not mean that the fairies stumble and fall.
‘Flank’ means be at the side of something.
Boots stand beside the door where the child had imagined horsemen.
‘Rippling’ describes water moving in small waves.
The beautiful blue streams are gone from the child’s view.
In their place are a bath and a water-can, a container for water.
The change is striking: a whole flowing landscape has become ordinary things in a room.
The repeated negatives—‘No fairies’ and ‘not horsemen’—draw attention to what the child misses.
I seek the magic land in vain
At seven, when I wake again.
Why does the child keep looking for the magic land?
The imagined world was vivid and exciting, and the child wants to find it again.
But ‘in vain’ tells us that the search is unsuccessful.
The child seems disappointed and longs for the dream world.
That is an interpretation supported by the repeated search and the contrast with the ordinary room.
The poem does not say that imagination has disappeared forever.
It describes what the child cannot find on waking at this moment.
Let’s connect the two halves.
In the first stanza, the child finds the dream world clearly in the mind.
In the second, the child seeks it in the room and cannot find it.
Castle and chair.
Garden and carpet.
Horsemen and boots.
Streams and a bath with a water-can.
These paired details make the contrast easy to picture.
The poem explores the power of a child’s imagination and the disappointment of returning to ordinary surroundings.
The title, ‘A Child’s Thought’, keeps our attention on the child’s inner experience.
First, personification.
In ‘the castle frowned’, the castle receives a human action.
People can frown; buildings cannot literally do that.
The phrase makes the castle seem stern or forbidding, as though it has a personality.
Second, listen to the rhyme: ‘bed’ and ‘head’; ‘round’ and ‘found’; ‘tower’ and ‘bower’.
These matching sounds give the verse a pleasing musical pattern.
We find rhyming pairs in the second stanza too, such as ‘floor’ and ‘door’.
Third, repetition.
‘At seven’ returns, but bedtime becomes waking time.
The first stanza begins and ends with going to bed.
The second begins and ends with waking again.
Each stanza has ten lines.
This balanced shape helps us notice what changes: the world the child experiences, and the child’s feelings about it.
Let’s check our understanding.
Say your answer aloud, or pause the video if you need more time.
One.
Name two things in the child’s imaginary world.
Where does the child find these pictures?
You could name castles, dragons, magical gardens, ladies in a tower or bower, horsemen, or streams.
The child finds the pictures in the mind at bedtime.
Two.
What figure of speech is used in ‘the castle frowned’?
Explain how it works.
It is personification.
A castle is given the human action of frowning, making it seem stern or forbidding.
A complete answer gives the name of the device and explains the words.
Three.
How do the child’s feelings change on waking?
Support your answer with a phrase from the poem.
At bedtime, the child seems delighted by the vivid magical pictures.
On waking, the child seems disappointed and wishes to find that world again.
The phrase ‘seek the magic land in vain’ supports this answer: the child looks for it without success.
Stevenson lets us experience a familiar feeling: an imaginary world can seem wonderfully real, even though it exists in our minds.
Remember the contrast between bedtime and morning, the ordinary objects that replace the dream scenes, and the child’s unsuccessful search for the magic land.
For a small creative challenge, choose one ordinary object in your room.
What might it become in an imaginary adventure?
Keep that picture in your head—and perhaps turn it into a line of your own.
